metadata.title: The Formatting Trap
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper development log, Week 6 — replacing strict string equality with a semantic parser, so stylistically different spellings of the same quantity stop registering as hallucinations while genuine magnitude errors and malicious payloads still get caught.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal, and this video is about teaching the Provenance Gatekeeper how to read. Until now our A.I. security layer used a strict equality check. If the ground truth was five million, and the model wrote five million with a dollar sign, the system flagged it as a hallucination. This week we fix that false positive by building a deterministic normalization engine.

beats.honesty_note: The string comparison shown is literally false in Python — verified. It illustrates the false-positive class the script describes; no claimed false-positive RATE is given, because the script reports none.

beats.narration_text: A verifier that cannot tell a formatting difference from a factual one is not strict. It is noisy — and a noisy verifier gets switched off. Week six taught the Gatekeeper to compare quantities instead of characters.

props.text:
A strict checker is a safe checker.
Compare quantities, not characters.

beats.authoring_note: Single-word trigger: BrutalistHesitantWriter matches whitespace-delimited word cores only. 'safe'->'noisy' is the reel's actual misconception — strictness reads as rigour until it produces false positives nobody trusts.

beats.narration_text: To build enterprise-grade evaluation logic you cannot rely on rigid string matching. We refactored the Python backend to include a dedicated semantic parser. Before comparing the model's claim to the ChromaDB ledger, the new code strips commas and dollar signs, maps text suffixes like M or K onto their multipliers, and converts both sides into standard float values.

stages.name: REGEX EXTRACTION
stages.detail: pull the digits, keep the suffix — it carries the magnitude

stages.name: FLOAT CONVERSION
stages.detail: both sides become numbers before anything is judged

beats.authoring_note: NARRATION CORRECTED FROM THE SCRIPT. The script says the parser 'strips out … text suffixes like M or K'. Stripping the M turns 5.0M into 5.0 — and the script's own Scene 4 requires 5.0M to PASS against a five-million ground truth, which is only possible if the suffix is MAPPED to a multiplier rather than removed. Narration now says 'maps text suffixes onto their multipliers'. See SOURCES.md.

beats.narration_text: So let's write that parser, then throw the worst thing an attacker could send at it and see whether it refuses politely or takes the service down with it.

props.command: Write parse_financial_number(text) -> float | None. It must read $5,000,000.00, 5.0M and "exactly 5 million" as the same value, and return None — never raise — for DROP TABLE or N/A.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: BASK is the ask, B03 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW). Added after the first audio pass, when the omission was caught.

beats.narration_text: The beauty of this parser is what happens when it fails. If an adversarial user injects a S.Q.L. command, or the model hallucinates a non-numerical string like N slash A, the regex engine yields a clean, controlled null. The system categorizes that as a data type error and blocks the payload — without crashing the server.
beats.new_visual_element: The hostile input, the parser, and the controlled null

show.event: left panel lands: the adversarial payload as received
on 'injects a SQL command', the command highlights terracotta IN PLACE
note lands beneath: no digits anywhere — nothing to extract
right panel reveals parse_financial_number line by line
stamp lands: None — a controlled refusal, not an exception

props.hotNote: no digits anywhere — nothing to extract
props.code:
m = re.search(r'([\d,]*\.?\d+)\s*([KMB])?',
              text, re.I)
if not m:
    return None          # controlled

val = float(m.group(1).replace(',', ''))
if m.group(2):
    val *= SUFFIX[m.group(2).upper()]
return val
props.stampSub: payload blocked, server still running — a return value, not an exception

beats.honesty_note: Verified by execution: the parser returns None for 'DROP TABLE logs;' and for 'N/A', and does not raise. The script's claim that the regex 'yields a clean, controlled null' is accurate for this implementation.

beats.narration_text: When we run the updated stress test, the results hold. The Gatekeeper recognises stylistically different formats as mathematically identical, letting valid data through — while still intercepting genuine magnitude errors and malicious payloads. Four point five M is not a formatting difference. It is a different number, and it fails.

props.sparkLine: Same number, five spellings, one verdict.

beats.honesty_note: Every PARSED value in this table was produced by RUNNING the parser, not by hand. $5,000,000.00 / 5.0M / exactly 5 million -> 5000000.0 (PASS); 4.5M -> 4500000.0 (FAIL, magnitude); DROP TABLE logs; -> None (FAIL, data type). These are exactly the verdicts the script's Scene 4 asserts. The 48-case count is ILLUSTRATIVE — no real suite size was supplied.

beats.narration_text: So update your evaluation logic. Build a regex parser that sanitizes unpredictable model strings into strict data types before you run your comparative math. Deterministic security requires deterministic inputs.

props.title: main.py
props.code:
def parse_financial_number(
        text: str) -> float | None:
    ...

# The line that does the real work:
SUFFIX = {'K': 1e3, 'M': 1e6, 'B': 1e9}

# Strip the $ and the commas.
# MAP the suffix — never strip it.
# Return None instead of raising.
#
# Deterministic security requires
# deterministic inputs.

beats.authoring_note: 'MAP the suffix — never strip it' is the reel's addition, and it is the correction this whole reel turns on. The script's Scene 2 says strip; its Scene 4 expectations require map.

beats.narration_text: And once your parser is in, here is the prompt worth running. Give a model your parser and your ground-truth values, and ask for claims that are factually WRONG but still parse to exactly the right float. Those are the hallucinations your new, smarter checker now waves straight through.

props.command: Here is my number parser and my ground-truth value. Give me claims that are factually WRONG but parse to exactly the correct float — wrong period, wrong entity, wrong currency, right digits. Those are the ones loosening the check just let through.

beats.authoring_note: The handoff deliberately attacks the week's own improvement: every loosened check buys false-negative risk, and the reel should say so rather than end on a victory lap.

beats.narration_text: A checker that cries wolf gets ignored. A checker that compares quantities gets used. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
